## Linear Regression Modeling
```{python}
from statsmodels.formula.api import ols
model=ols("body_mass_g ~ bill_length_mm", data=data)
model=model.fit()
```
### Model Summary and Statistical Results
```{python}
print(model.summary())
```
### Regression Visualization
```{python}
sns.regplot(x="bill_length_mm", y="body_mass_g", data=data)
plt.show()
```
## Regression Assumption Diagnostics 
### Residual Distribution Analysis -Normality
```{python}
sns.histplot(data=model.resid, kde=True)
plt.title("Histogram of residuals")
plt.show()
```
### Normality Assessment Using Q–Q Plot
```{python}
import statsmodels.api as sm
sm.qqplot(model.resid, line="s")
plt.show()
```
### Residuals vs Fitted Values Analysis
```{python}
sns.scatterplot(x=model.fittedvalues, y=model.resid)
plt.axhline()
plt.show()
```
## Conclusion
## Conclusion

A simple linear regression model was developed to evaluate the relationship between **bill length (mm)** and **body mass (g)** for Adelie and Gentoo penguins.

The model produced an **R² value of 0.769**, indicating that approximately **76.9% of the variation in penguin body mass can be explained by bill length alone**. This suggests a strong linear relationship between the two variables.

The regression coefficient for **bill length (141.19)** indicates that, on average, **for every 1 mm increase in bill length, body mass is predicted to increase by approximately 141 grams**.

The predictor was found to be **statistically significant** (**p < 0.001**), providing evidence that bill length contributes meaningfully to predicting body mass.

Residual diagnostics further suggest that the regression assumptions are reasonably satisfied:
- Residuals appear approximately normally distributed
- No major systematic patterns were observed
- The model demonstrates acceptable fit for simple linear regression

Overall, the analysis indicates that **bill length is a strong predictor of penguin body mass within the selected species group.**
